optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The dot inside the bracketed SQL column name makes default mapping navigate to billing's nested code B2.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The brackets delimit one SQL name, billing.code. Without an explicit column_path, OPENJSON matches that name to the literal top-level key, whose value is A7. The existing nested B2 is not the selected property.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: With @payload = N'{"billing.code":"B2","billing":{"code":"A7"}}', the unchanged query returns B2. For the original input instead, WITH ([billing.code] nvarchar(10) '$.billing.code') would select B2. The former changes the input; the latter changes the projection.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Remarks directly distinguishes dotted WITH column names from explicit nested column paths. colName uses the default literal name unless column_path overrides it. Thus B2 can be a real result under the stated alternate input or nested-path projection, but not this frozen query.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Default mapping cannot resolve the dotted column name and therefore returns SQL NULL.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The exact literal billing.code key is present with the short scalar A7. A dot does not invalidate this default name match, so neither an absent-property nor a nonscalar-path NULL condition applies.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: With @payload = N'{"billing":{"code":"B2"}}', SELECT [billing.code] FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH ([billing.code] nvarchar(10)); returns SQL NULL in default lax mode. The query is unchanged, but the required literal dotted key is absent.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Remarks permits literal dotted-name matching and identifies lax as the default missing-path mode. colName defines the exact default property lookup. Together these rules explain successful extraction here and NULL for the concrete nested-only input.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The shown scalar projection returns the nested billing object as the fragment {"code":"B2"}.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The query selects literal billing.code, not billing, and declares no AS JSON flag. The actual selected value is A7. Returning the nested object as a fragment instead requires an explicit billing path and the nvarchar(max) type mandated for AS JSON.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: SELECT [billing.code] FROM OPENJSON(N'{"billing":{"code":"B2"}}') WITH ([billing.code] nvarchar(max) '$.billing' AS JSON); returns the displayed object fragment. This is a deliberately different query, not an unchanged-query counterexample: both the path and fragment-capable projection are necessary.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The AS JSON and type sections require nvarchar(max) when preserving objects or arrays. column_path must select the desired property, while Remarks keeps a dotted default column name literal. These explicit contracts support the alternate fragment query, not silently changing the original projection.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The default WITH mapping reads A7 from the exact literal top-level key billing.code.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: This is supported, not incorrect. The bracketed output name matches the literal JSON key, no path override is supplied, and the selected value is scalar text compatible with nvarchar(10). The nested object's different code remains irrelevant.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: The displayed query correctly returns A7 for the given input. It also returns A7 unchanged when @payload = N'{"billing.code":"A7"}', demonstrating that the nested billing object is not a prerequisite for default dotted-name mapping.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Remarks directly documents matching a dotted WITH name to a key containing that dot and requiring a separate explicit path for nested traversal. The scalar projection and explicit-schema return contracts support A7 in the declared output column.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: OPENJSON (Transact-SQL): independently read Remarks' explicit distinction between literal dotted WITH names and nested column paths, together with colName, column_path, AS JSON and return-schema rules. A present literal scalar maps normally; a missing literal key can yield NULL in lax mode. Returning a nested object instead needs its explicit path and nvarchar(max) AS JSON. These sections establish both the actual A7 result and valid alternate contexts.

choiceReviews.rationale: B2 belongs to the nested billing object, but the bracketed column name supplies no nested JSON path. OPENJSON instead matches the literal billing.code key containing A7. The unchanged query would return B2 from N'{"billing.code":"B2","billing":{"code":"A7"}}'; alternatively, an explicit '$.billing.code' projection would reach B2 in the original input. Each concrete countercontext changes a frozen premise, so neither makes this choice correct for the displayed query.

A literal dot does not prevent default name matching, and the exact billing.code key is present with scalar A7. The absence condition needed for this NULL answer therefore does not hold. With N'{"billing":{"code":"B2"}}', the unchanged SELECT and WITH clause would yield SQL NULL under default lax handling because only the nested key exists. This valid missing-literal-key case is different from the supplied complete input.

The selected property is the literal scalar A7, not the billing object, and no AS JSON flag requests a fragment. A valid countercontext is SELECT [billing.code] FROM OPENJSON(N'{"billing":{"code":"B2"}}') WITH ([billing.code] nvarchar(max) '$.billing' AS JSON);, which returns the displayed object. That explicitly different projection supplies both the object path and required max-length fragment type. It must not be represented as an outcome of the unchanged query.

The output name billing.code is a single bracket-delimited SQL identifier. Without a column_path override, OPENJSON matches it to the exact top-level JSON key of that name and projects its scalar A7 into nvarchar(10). The nested billing.code path is a different location and is not implicitly traversed. The same query also returns A7 from N'{"billing.code":"A7"}', showing that the extra nested object does not participate in the selected mapping.
